prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in this tunable moire platform

statement.case_for: After the full exchange I keep B022 as a single three-person part. The committee has split four to four between B022 and B012, and no one disputes the existence of the phenomenology: flat bands at small twist, correlated insulators and superconducting domes are reproduced by many independent groups in several device geometries. What B022 offers that no other entry does is a new, tunable regime of quantum matter in which twist angle and gate density turn a hard many-body problem into a controlled experiment, and in which a band-structure calculation pointed to where to look. The chair asks whether the citation can be restricted to what is established. I think it can and must: flat bands predicted at the magic angle by the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, and correlated insulating and superconducting states discovered experimentally in 2018, with no claim about the pairing mechanism and no suggestion that theory predicted the correlated phases. Worded that way the citation rests on what is secure and the open mechanism question stays outside the prize.
statement.case_against: I take the objections from the other camp seriously. The field is about eight years old and the superconducting mechanism, sample variability and the nature of several correlated states are unsettled; waiting would improve both interpretation and attribution. The experimental credit is also the weakest part of my configuration: Cory Dean's hBN-encapsulated devices, the first author of the 2018 papers, and the groups of Young, Yacoby, Efetov and Yazdani are all outside the three names, and I cannot verify the author record from the supplied material. If that record showed that the experimental discovery cannot fairly be summarised by Jarillo-Herrero alone, the case for B022 would weaken materially and B012, with its tighter two-name credit and years of independent confirmation, would become the better prize this year. I therefore regard B022 as stronger on scientific originality and B012 as stronger on attribution and maturity, and I am choosing on the first while conceding the second.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the optical lattice clock is the clearest case of a result that moved a measurement frontier, with unusually clean attribution (Katori's magic-wavelength condition, Ye's 10^-18 realisation) and no maturity concern, and treats the pending SI redefinition as supporting evidence of impact.
responses.response: I agree with Kroll on attribution and maturity and have not weakened that view. Where I still differ is on what the prize is for. The clock is a superb improvement in how well a quantity can be measured, and its largest consequences, geodesy, tests of constants and the second, are still prospective, while B022 has already produced a new field with a distinct set of phases. Kroll's point that the moire field is young and the mechanism open has moved me to restrict the citation to the prediction of flat bands and the observed correlated states. I would accept B012 if the experimental author record for B022 turns out to be a real problem, but I do not think a pending redefinition of the second should weigh in either direction.

responses.point: Johansson moved from quantum key distribution to the lattice clock, ranks B022 sixth for prematurity, and asks whether the SI redefinition must happen first and whether priority for the magic-wavelength proposal over contemporaneous work has been checked.
responses.response: Johansson's priority question is a fair one and I cannot answer it from the supplied material; it is the same kind of check I would want on the B022 side, so I do not hold it against B012 alone. On prematurity I disagree with ranking B022 sixth. Maturity in our practice means independent confirmation, and flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity have been reproduced across laboratories and device types, which is the evidence we asked of the clock. What is immature is the mechanism, and the citation does not claim it. I also note that Johansson has moved off his opening choice for lack of colleague support, and that I would not want the same mistake of carrying a position on conviction alone to apply to my own.

responses.point: Lindroth supports the lattice clock as a single well-defined invention with the cleanest two-name credit, but worries that a Katori-Ye citation could imply that trapped-ion clocks and other lattice-clock groups rank lower, and that much of the value is still prospective.
responses.response: Lindroth's ion-clock concern is the strongest reservation about B012 and it is the mirror image of my concern about B022, since both citations draw a line through a larger community. I think both can be handled by wording around the specific architecture, as Kroll and she propose, but that does not remove the exclusion, it only avoids implying a ranking. She also concedes that she may be underweighting the pull of a large new field, which I think is correct, and I would ask the committee to treat the breadth of what moire systems opened, not only the cleanliness of credit, as part of the discovery criterion.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022 as a clean theory-to-experiment story and strongly correlated electrons with tunable parameters, and acknowledges that other theory groups also worked on flat bands and moire structures.
responses.response: I agree on tunability, and I accept Mehlig's acknowledgment that other theorists contributed; that is part of why the theory credit has to be limited to the continuum model and the magic-angle flat bands. The point where I stay more cautious than he does is the claim that this is a clean theory-to-experiment story. The continuum model located the flat bands but did not predict insulators or superconductivity, so the story is a calculation that told experimentalists where to look, followed by a discovery nobody had computed. I think that is still a strong and unusual case, but the citation should say exactly that.

responses.point: As chair, Pearce moved from IceCube to B022, asks that the author record of the first 2018 reports be examined before the final vote, and reports finding no two-part split that is fair to both the B022 and B012 credited names.
responses.response: I support Pearce's request to examine the 2018 author record, and I think it is the single most decisive open item. I also agree that no two-part configuration is fair: three names for B022 and two for B012 would be five people, above the cap, and trimming either side would make the credit arbitrary. I therefore remain with one part. Pearce's observation that his move away from B013 rested on AMANDA and DUMAND credit and partial source identification matches my own collaboration-scale reservation about IceCube, so I do not see that entry returning.

uncertainties: Whether the author and credit record of the 2018 B022 papers, including Dean's group and the first author, supports Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero as an acceptable allocation; I cannot verify it and it would change my ranking.
Whether eight years is sufficient maturity given the unresolved pairing mechanism, or whether waiting would settle interpretation and credit.
Whether a lattice-clock citation can be worded without implicitly ranking it above trapped-ion clocks, and whether priority for the magic-wavelength proposal has been checked.
Whether my own closeness to band-structure methods makes me overvalue the theory side of B022.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional link to any shortlisted candidate is documented. My field of electronic-structure theory and magnetism at Uppsala is methodologically close to the band-structure side of B022, which I flag as a possible disciplinary preference, and I have no tie to B012 or the other alternatives. I would not seek recusal but disclose the proximity.
